Raymond was heartened by the keen delight of returning health. As general of the Athenians, he felt himself in a station equal to his ambition; and in anticipating the capture of Constantinople, he looked towards an achievement that would stand as a marker amid the wilderness of ages, a deed without parallel in human records. A city rich in historic memories, whose beautiful situation astonished the world, and which for centuries had been a fortress of the Moslems, would be delivered from bondage and barbarism and restored to a people renowned for genius, civilization, and love of freedom. Perdita reposed upon his recovered companionship, his affection, his hopes and glory, as a Sybarite upon a sumptuous couch. Each thought was rapture, each feeling seemed immersed in a soothing and congenial atmosphere.

We reached Kishan on July the seventh. Throughout our journey the weather had remained serene. Every morning before daybreak we departed our nightly camp and watched the shadows withdraw from hill and valley before the golden magnificence of the approaching sun. With their national liveliness, the soldiers accompanying us delighted enthusiastically in nature’s beauty. Triumphant music greeted the rising star of day, and birdsong, heard in fragments, filled the pauses between the strains. At midday we raised our tents in a shaded valley or beneath the sheltering trees of a mountain wood, where a brook murmuring over stones invited welcome slumber. Our evening progress was quieter, yet more delightful, than the morning’s restless animation. When the band played, the musicians instinctively selected airs of gentler feeling: a lover’s farewell or a lament for separation would give way at last to a solemn hymn, answering the evening’s peaceful beauty and lifting the soul towards lofty and religious contemplation. Often every sound ceased so that we could hear the nightingale, while fireflies danced in luminous rhythm and the aziolo’s gentle coo promised the travellers fine weather. When we entered a valley, tender shadows and richly tinted rocks surrounded us. When we crossed a mountain, Greece unfolded below like a living map, her celebrated peaks piercing the heavens and her rivers drawing silver threads across the fertile country. We English travellers gazed almost breathlessly in delight at this glorious prospect, so unlike the restrained colours and melancholy charms of our native landscapes. After we left Macedonia, the rich but flat plains of Thrace offered less beauty, though our journey continued to hold our interest. An advance guard announced our coming, and the countryfolk were soon astir to pay Lord Raymond honour.

Many American women, on leaving their homeland, begin to look permanently unwell, thinking this a sign of European elegance. Mrs. Otis had never made that mistake. She enjoyed excellent health and a truly remarkable supply of energy and good spirits. In many ways, indeed, she was quite English, a fine example of how much we now share with America—everything, of course, except language. Her eldest son was named Washington in a patriotic moment that his parents had enjoyed and he never stopped regretting. He was a fair-haired, fairly handsome young man. He had prepared himself for American diplomacy by leading the German dance at the Newport Casino for three seasons running, and even in London he was known as an excellent dancer. His only weaknesses were gardenias and the aristocracy. In other matters he was extremely sensible. Miss Virginia E. Otis was a girl of fifteen, graceful and lovely as a young deer, with a fine, free look in her large blue eyes. She was a splendid rider. Once she had raced old Lord Bilton on her pony twice around the park, winning by a length and a half just before the Achilles statue. The young Duke of Cheshire was so delighted that he proposed to her immediately. His guardians sent him back to Eton that same night, crying bitterly. After Virginia came the twins, usually called ‘The Stars and Stripes’ because they were always being whipped. They were delightful boys and, apart from the worthy Minister, the family’s only true republicans.

Canterville Chase stood seven miles from Ascot, the nearest railway station, so Mr. Otis had sent a telegram requesting an open carriage to meet them. They began the drive in high spirits. It was a beautiful July evening, and the air carried the faint scent of pine woods. Sometimes they heard a wood pigeon lingering over its own sweet song, or saw a pheasant’s shining breast deep among the rustling ferns. Small squirrels peeped at them from the beech trees as they passed. Rabbits darted through the bushes and across mossy little hills, their white tails raised. But as they turned into the avenue leading to Canterville Chase, clouds suddenly covered the sky. A strange stillness seemed to settle over the air, and a large flock of rooks flew silently overhead. Before they reached the house, several heavy drops of rain had fallen.

An old woman stood on the steps to welcome them, neatly dressed in black silk, with a white cap and apron.

Young Charles Bates was so horrified by Sikes’s crime that he began to wonder whether an honest life was, after all, the best one. Having decided that it certainly was, he left the places of his past behind, determined to make up for that past through a new way of life. For a while he struggled hard and suffered greatly. But his cheerful nature and good intentions brought him success in the end. After working as a farmer’s labourer and a delivery man’s boy, he is now the happiest young cattle farmer in all Northamptonshire.

And now the hand writing these words hesitates as it nears the end of its task, wishing to spin the thread of these adventures a little longer.

I would gladly stay a while with a few of the people whose lives I have shared so long, and share their happiness by trying to describe it. I would show Rose Maylie in the beauty and grace of her early womanhood, bringing a soft, gentle light to her quiet life, a light that fell on everyone who shared it and shone into their hearts. I would picture her as the life and joy of gatherings by the fire and cheerful summer parties. I would follow her through the hot fields at noon, and hear her sweet voice speaking softly on an evening walk beneath the moon. I would watch her kindness and generosity toward others, and her smiling, tireless attention to her duties at home. I would show her and her dead sister’s child happy in their love, spending hours together remembering the friends they had so sadly lost. I would bring back once more the happy little faces gathered around her knees and listen to their merry chatter. I would recall her clear laugh and the tear of sympathy shining in her gentle blue eye. These things, and a thousand expressions, smiles, thoughts, and ways of speaking—I would gladly recall every one.

There is no need to tell how Mr. Brownlow went on teaching his adopted child day by day, filling his mind with knowledge and loving him more deeply as his character developed and showed the promising beginnings of all he hoped the boy would become. Nor need I tell how he discovered fresh reminders of his early friend in the boy, stirring old memories that were sad, yet sweet and comforting. Nor how the two orphans, who had suffered so much hardship, remembered its lessons by showing mercy to others, loving each other, and offering heartfelt thanks to Him who had guarded and saved them. These things require no further telling.
